node.label: Nancy Leys Stepan
node.date_label: The Idea of Race in Science (1982) · “Race and Gender” (1986) · The Hour of Eugenics (1991) · Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) · Eradication (2011)
node.description: In The Hour of Eugenics (1991), Nancy Leys Stepan argued that eugenics in Brazil, Argentina and Mexico was remade through local scientific, political and cultural conditions. Race, gender, reproduction and public health therefore belong within histories of nationhood, rather than a model of Latin American science simply copying Europe. Philippa Levine credits the book with revealing the variety of eugenics, including programmes of housing and maternal care. Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) studies how images helped construct the tropics; David Arnold’s review, excerpted by the publisher, praises its advance in interpreting tropicality. Eradication (2011) places campaigns against disease alongside debates over primary health care.

node.scope_note: “Race and Gender” (1986) is listed bibliographically; its text is unread. Read selected pages of the 1998 English medical-history review, the citizenship article’s abstract, publisher descriptions and bibliographic records, Levine’s interview passage, and the publisher-hosted Social History of Medicine review excerpt. Nature’s Body and the complete Arnold review were not read. Selected monographs were not read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science' (1986; cited in a 1996 reprint), Stepan likens the role of a metaphor in the logic of science to that of a Kuhnian paradigm, as Paul Bartha reports in By Parallel Reasoning (2010).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Abridged reprint, reader p. 45 and p. 49 n. 37: ‘programme of research’. Names Structure and Kuhn’s metaphor essay. Selected primary passage; original Isis version and Kuhn texts uncollated. Not a claim of wholesale theoretical allegiance.
proposed_edges.map_label: Likens scientific metaphor to a Kuhnian paradigm

proposed_edges.relationship: In a 2016 interview, Levine credits The Hour of Eugenics (1991) as the first book to show a pro-natal 'other mode of eugenics' that sought better births through housing, medical care and antenatal care.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Five Books interview, section 4, question naming the 1991 book and answer beginning I think it is important to ask: ‘this other way too’. Interview date not displayed. Published reception, not proof that Stepan supplied Levine’s entire framework. Book unread in full.
proposed_edges.map_label: Levine: first to show pro-natal eugenics

proposed_edges.relationship: In his 2002 review of Picturing Tropical Nature (2001), Arnold praises the book as a major advance in interpreting tropicality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Chicago publisher excerpt, description ending: ‘carries forward a field’. Excerpt credited only to Social History of Medicine; 15(1) contents name Arnold, pp. 175–176. Attribution joins these exact book/journal records; complete review unread. Evaluation only, not an established intellectual debt.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science” (1986) takes up the debated role of metaphor and analogy in scientific theory, against science’s traditional standing as the repository of nonmetaphorical, politically neutral knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Selected primary reprint, reader p. 42, Metaphoric interactions: ‘constituent elements of science’. Reader is abridged; original version uncollated.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Tropical Medicine and Public Health in Latin America” (1998) organizes medical history around political priorities, laboratory science, international agencies and race.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: English essay, pp. 104–106, especially the four-theme statement on p. 106 and question ‘who defines the public’. Selected review pages read; reviewed books unread. Contribution to a field, not evidence of a unified school.

proposed_edges.relationship: Picturing Tropical Nature (2001) studies tropical nature as a European and American imaginative construct, including anti-tropicalism's role in an emerging environmentalist sensibility and the imagery of tropical medicine.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Davis excerpt in Cornell’s UTP distributor page, Reviews, web lines 71–75, explicitly identifies ‘environmental history’. Publisher description also discusses environmentalist sensibility. Named review excerpt only; book and complete Davis review unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In 'Tropical Medicine and Public Health in Latin America' (1998), Stepan sets Latin American medical history beside postcolonial questions about colonies and science, arguing that the colonial framework developed in studies of India and Africa is of limited use for the region's independent countries.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: English essay p. 104: ‘uneasy fit’ and ‘limited use’. Opening acknowledges postcolonial questions but stresses political independence and changing centres of medical reference. Qualified regional criticism, not rejection of postcolonial history. Selected primary page; reviewed books unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Colonial framework of limited use for Latin America

proposed_edges.relationship: In his 2003 review of Picturing Tropical Nature (2001), MacKenzie argues that Stepan does not follow her argument through to its logical conclusion: the tropics were never portrayed as a single entity opposed to temperate regions, as empathetic travellers and tropical plants in European winter gardens and greenhouses show.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: MacKenzie's complete review, AHR 108(1) (2003), pp. 150–151, read in the publisher's two publicly displayed first-page preview images. The first is linked from his own article; the second, containing the continuation and his signature on p. 151, is linked from the adjacent Harvey J. Kaye review of Ellen Fitzpatrick. On p. 151 MacKenzie praises Stepan's treatment of tropical medicine and medical photography, then argues that she leaves the complexity of tropical representations insufficiently developed. His examples include sympathetic travellers, tropical plants in European homes, and differences within tropical and temperate regions. The claim concerns this substantive criticism; it does not rest on his praise alone. Stepan's book itself remains unread. The checked URL is the publisher-supplied preview image of p. 151, linked at https://academic.oup.com/ahr/article/108/1/151/22648.
proposed_edges.map_label: Ambiguity in representations of the tropics

proposed_edges.relationship: Nancy Leys Stepan's ‘Race and Gender: The Role of Analogy in Science’ (1986) contributed a historical analysis of race–gender analogies that Mary E. John engaged in Discrepant Dislocations (1996), in her discussion of gender and feminist theory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read John's sustained discussion on pp. 87–90 and note 30 in the publisher's archive. John credits Stepan's historical account and considers its implications while criticizing Sandra Harding's analogies. This supports a bounded contribution to gender analysis, not founding the field. John cites the 1990 anthology version; the original 1986 publication was checked on the journal's own page. Stepan's full original article was not read. John has no eligible endpoint, so no person-to-person edge is proposed.
